title: How Rob Walling bought, grew, and sold HitTail, and what it taught him
summary: Rob recounts buying the SaaS app HitTail, growing revenue 10x in 15 months, then selling it via a broker to focus on Drip. He draws four lessons: stair-stepping, what money actually enables, buying beats building, and the leverage available to solo founders.

principles.text: Start small and climb to larger, harder opportunities as skills, funds, and confidence grow (stair-stepping).
principles.quote: Stair Stepping as an optimal approach for maximizing results while minimizing your chance of failure. It’s not the fastest path, but a predictable one.

principles.text: Experience from a smaller step is what makes a bigger, more competitive step survivable.
principles.quote: Had I tried to launch Drip in 2011 without the experience, skills, funds and confidence I gained from growing HitTail, I would have had my ass handed to me.

principles.text: Buying a product that already has product/market fit saves 12-18 months and removes pre-PMF anxiety.
principles.quote: acquiring an application that already has product/market fit puts you 12-18 months ahead of starting from scratch.

principles.text: Once a new venture's growth curve dominates, divest side projects to focus fully on it.
principles.quote: at a certain point Drip’s growth curve became such that it didn’t make sense for me to focus even a few hours a month on any other products.

principles.text: Money's value is breathing room (generosity, time control, security), not stuff.
principles.quote: I don’t think you need buckets of money to be happy. And, in my experience, “more stuff” is a ridiculous reason to seek more money.

principles.text: Cheap tools and global labor give a solo founder huge leverage today.
principles.quote: I believe today is the best time in history to be a founder. And it’s especially easier for a single founder given the power of outsourcing and today’s global labor pool.
